source: Not seldom in this life, when, on the right side, fortune’s favourites sail close by us, we, though all adroop before, catch somewhat of the rushing breeze, and joyfully feel our bagging sails fill out. So seemed it with the Pequod. For next day after encountering the gay Bachelor, whales were seen and four were slain; and one of them by Ahab.

It was far down the afternoon; and when all the spearings of the crimson fight were done: and floating in the lovely sunset sea and sky, sun and whale both stilly died together; then, such a sweetness and such plaintiveness, such inwreathing orisons curled up in that rosy air, that it almost seemed as if far over from the deep green convent valleys of the Manilla isles, the Spanish land-breeze, wantonly turned sailor, had gone to sea, freighted with these vesper hymns.

Soothed again, but only soothed to deeper gloom, Ahab, who had sterned off from the whale, sat intently watching his final wanings from the now tranquil boat. For that strange spectacle observable in all sperm whales dying—the turning sunwards of the head, and so expiring—that strange spectacle, beheld of such a placid evening, somehow to Ahab conveyed a wondrousness unknown before.

“He turns and turns him to it,—how slowly, but how steadfastly, his homage-rendering and invoking brow, with his last dying motions. He too worships fire; most faithful, broad, baronial vassal of the sun!—Oh that these too-favouring eyes should see these too-favouring sights. Look! here, far water-locked; beyond all hum of human weal or woe; in these most candid and impartial seas; where to traditions no rocks furnish tablets; where for long Chinese ages, the billows have still rolled on speechless and unspoken to, as stars that shine upon the Niger’s unknown source; here, too, life dies sunwards full of faith; but see! no sooner dead, than death whirls round the corpse, and it heads some other way.

“Oh, thou dark Hindoo half of nature, who of drowned bones hast builded thy separate throne somewhere in the heart of these unverdured seas; thou art an infidel, thou queen, and too truly speakest to me in the wide-slaughtering Typhoon, and the hushed burial of its after calm. Nor has this thy whale sunwards turned his dying head, and then gone round again, without a lesson to me.

“Oh, trebly hooped and welded hip of power! Oh, high aspiring, rainbowed jet!—that one strivest, this one jettest all in vain! In vain, oh whale, dost thou seek intercedings with yon all-quickening sun, that only calls forth life, but gives it not again. Yet dost thou, darker half, rock me with a prouder, if a darker faith. All thy unnamable imminglings float beneath me here; I am buoyed by breaths of once living things, exhaled as air, but water now.

“Then hail, for ever hail, O sea, in whose eternal tossings the wild fowl finds his only rest. Born of earth, yet suckled by the sea; though hill and valley mothered me, ye billows are my foster-brothers!”

modern_en.title: Chapter 116 — The Dying Whale
paragraphs: It happens often enough in this life that when fortune's favorites sail close by us on the right side, we, though we were drooping before, catch something of their rushing breeze and joyfully feel our slack sails fill out. So it seemed with the Pequod. On the day after she met the cheerful Bachelor, whales were sighted and four were killed, one of them by Ahab.

It was far into the afternoon; and when all the spearings of the crimson fight were done, and, floating in the lovely sunset sea and sky, sun and whale both silently died together — then such sweetness and such plaintiveness, such wreathing prayers, curled up into that rosy air that it almost seemed as if, far over from the deep green convent valleys of the Manila isles, the Spanish land-breeze, wantonly turned sailor, had gone to sea freighted with these vesper hymns.

Soothed again, but only soothed to deeper gloom, Ahab, who had backed off from the whale, sat intently watching its final wanings from the now tranquil boat. For that strange spectacle observable in all sperm whales dying — the turning sunward of the head, and so expiring — that strange spectacle, seen on such a placid evening, somehow conveyed to Ahab a wondrousness unknown before.

"He turns and turns himself to it — how slowly, but how steadfastly, his homage-rendering and invoking brow, with his last dying motions. He too worships fire; most faithful, broad, baronial vassal of the sun! Oh, that these too-favoring eyes should see these too-favoring sights. Look! Here, far water-locked; beyond all hum of human weal or woe; in these most candid and impartial seas; where no rocks furnish tablets for traditions; where for long Chinese ages the billows have still rolled on speechless and unspoken to, like stars that shine upon the Niger's unknown source — here, too, life dies sunward full of faith; but see! No sooner dead than death whirls round the corpse, and it heads some other way.

"Oh, you dark Hindu half of nature, who have built your separate throne of drowned bones somewhere in the heart of these unverdured seas; you are an infidel, you queen, and too truly you speak to me in the wide-slaughtering Typhoon, and the hushed burial of its after-calm. Nor has this whale of yours turned his dying head sunward, and then gone round again, without a lesson to me.

"Oh, trebly hooped and welded hip of power! Oh, high aspiring, rainbowed jet! The one strives, the other jets, all in vain! In vain, oh whale, do you seek intercession with the all-quickening sun, that only calls forth life but does not give it again. Yet you, darker half, rock me with a prouder, if a darker faith. All your unnamable imminglings float beneath me here; I am buoyed by breaths of once living things, exhaled as air, but water now.

"Then hail, forever hail, O sea, in whose eternal tossing the wild bird finds its only rest. I was born of earth, yet nursed by the sea; though hill and valley mothered me, you rolling waves are my foster-brothers!"

modern_da.title: Kapitel 116 — Den døende hval
paragraphs: Det sker ofte nok her i livet, at når lykkens yndlinge sejler tæt forbi os på den rette side, fanger vi, selv om vi hang med hovedet før, noget af deres susende vind og mærker glade, hvordan vores slappe sejl fyldes ud. Sådan syntes det også at gå med Pequod. Dagen efter, at hun havde mødt den muntre Bachelor, blev der set hvaler, og fire blev dræbt, en af dem af Ahab.

Det var langt ud på eftermiddagen; og da alle stikkene i den blodrøde kamp var givet, og sol og hval, flydende på det dejlige solnedgangshav og himmel, tavst døde sammen — da steg der en sådan sødme og klagende ynk, sådanne snoede bønner, op i den rosenrøde luft, at det næsten var, som om den spanske landbrise, i vildt mod blevet sømand, var gået til søs, lastet med disse aftensange, langt derovre fra de dybgrønne klosterdale på Manilas øer.

Atter beroliget, men kun beroliget til dybere dysterhed, sad Ahab, der var roet bort fra hvalen, og iagttog intenst dens sidste svindende kræfter fra den nu rolige båd. For det besynderlige skue, som kan ses hos alle døende kaskelotter — at hovedet vender sig mod solen, og at de så udånder — det besynderlige skue, set på en så stille aften, gav på en eller anden måde Ahab en forunderlighed, han ikke havde kendt før.

»Han vender og vender sig mod den — hvor langsomt, men hvor standhaftigt, med sin hyldende og påkaldende pande, i sine sidste døende bevægelser. Også han tilbeder ilden; mest trofaste, brede, baroniske vasal under solen! Åh, at disse alt for gunstige øjne skal se disse alt for gunstige syn. Se! Her, langt indesluttet af vand; hinsides al summen af menneskers vel og ve; i disse mest ærlige og upartiske have; hvor ingen klipper yder tavler til overleveringer; hvor bølgerne i lange kinesiske tidsaldre stadig har rullet videre uden tale og uden at blive talt til, som stjerner, der skinner over Nigers ukendte kilde — her dør også livet mod solen, fuldt af tro; men se! Næppe er det dødt, før døden hvirvler rundt om liget, og det peger en anden vej.

»Åh, du mørke hinduiske halvdel af naturen, som har bygget din særlige trone af druknede knogler et sted i hjertet af disse ugrønne have; du er en vantro, du dronning, og alt for sandt taler du til mig i den vidt slagtende tyfon og i den dæmpede jordfæstelse i stilheden efter den. Og denne din hval har ikke vendt sit døende hoved mod solen og så drejet rundt igen uden en lærdom til mig.

»Åh, trefold bundne og svejsede magtens hofte! Åh, højtstræbende, regnbuede stråle! Den ene stræber, den anden sprøjter, begge forgæves! Forgæves, åh hval, søger du forbøn hos den alt vækkende sol, der kun kalder livet frem, men ikke giver det igen. Dog du, mørkere halvdel, vugger mig med en stoltere, om end mørkere tro. Alle dine unævnelige iblandinger flyder under mig her; jeg bæres af ånde fra engang levende ting, udåndet som luft, men nu vand.

»Så vær hilset, evigt hilset, o hav, i hvis evige kasten den vilde fugl finder sin eneste hvile. Jeg blev født af jorden, men ammet af havet; skønt bakke og dal var mine mødre, er I rullende bølger mine fosterbrødre!«
